rationale: The exhausted prisoners have no helper, matching the other psalm's plea that God remain near because affliction is near and no one helps. Both make absence of human help part of an appeal for divine rescue.

Both link inability to take food with approaching death. Their symptoms differ: the psalm's sufferers abhor food, whereas Elihu's described sufferer desires food but cannot receive it; that difference is not erased.

The psalm compares the growth of families after relief from poverty to sheep. Ezekiel explicitly promises to multiply human beings like sheep and fill deserted cities, giving a particular parallel to the pastoral image of restored population.
The doubled declaration that the heart is ready and the resolve to sing and make music recur in Psalm56. Psalm107 adds in my glory without changing the shared declaration into a different occasion.
The speaker continues praying while receiving slander in place of love. Jesus' instruction to love enemies and pray for mistreaters supplies an explicit teaching parallel to that response.

The offender's loved curse returns to him and blessing remains distant. Later the speaker contrasts enemies' cursing with God's blessing; the repeated curse/blessing opposition distinguishes the two positions within this psalm.

relationship: Recognition of the Lord's hand in an event
rationale: The psalm asks that observers know the Lord's hand has acted. The foreigners' advisers propose watching the ark's route to determine whether His hand caused their harm; both distinguish divine action from another explanation without equating the events.

relationship: Judgment of nations and their dead
rationale: Both picture the Lord's judgment among nations with slaughter and exposed dead. Isaiah names wrath against the nations and their dead thrown out; the psalm speaks of a field filled with corpses and crushed heads.

relationship: The Lord exalted above earthly powers
rationale: Psalm112 declares the Lord high above all nations and His glory above the heavens. Psalm96 calls Him Most High over all the earth and exalted above all gods; the shared exaltation is clear while nations, gods and heavens remain different objects of comparison.

The psalm's opening recalls Israel leaving Egypt. Exodus narrates the Lord's host going out and the night vigil commemorating that departure; the psalm additionally characterizes the former people as foreign-speaking.

relationship: Repeated powerless hands, feet and throat
rationale: Psalm134's same unit also repeats the hands that do not touch, feet that do not walk and throat that produces no sound. The psalm's distributed clauses correspond to that longer target unit without creating separate target-range credits.

The people who fear the Lord, already described as hoping in Him, now receive blessing, small together with great. The repeated group links trust and blessing while adding the explicit inclusion of different ranks.

The psalm calls the Lord merciful and righteous and says God shows mercy. Exodus' proclamation describes Him as compassionate and merciful, preserving righteousness and showing mercy, supplying both attributes in its wording.
Both pair the Lord's mercy with the permanence of His truth. Psalm116 says truth remains for ever, while Psalm99 extends it through generation after generation.

The speaker surrounded by attackers corresponds to Psalm21's encirclement by a gathering of evildoers, pictured as dogs. Both portray surrounding hostility, with distinct animal imagery and without identifying the attackers.

relationship: A fall checked by the Lord's support
rationale: The pushed speaker is near falling when the Lord takes hold of him. Psalm36 likewise says a falling person will not be dashed down because the Lord supports his hand.
